strengths: Elegant and original integration of Krause's bounded-confidence consensus dynamics into the Transformer attention mechanism to naturally promote multi-cluster token coordination rather than global collapse.

Solid theoretical support connecting Krause Attention to both continuous-time particle dynamics and mean-field Wasserstein gradient flows, showing that the block-diagonal structure of the attention matrix rigorously preserves representational diversity.

Strong and consistent empirical performance across multiple modalities including image classification (ViT, Swin), autoregressive generation (MNIST, CIFAR-10), and LLM reasoning benchmarks (Llama3, Qwen1.5).
Substantial computational savings in practice, such as reducing Vision Transformer FLOPs by ~30% while achieving noticeable accuracy improvements (e.g., +1.65% on ImageNet-1K for ViT-S).
Highly clear exposition, well-structured arguments, and comprehensive appendices detailing proofs and training configurations.
weaknesses: The evaluation on LLMs is limited to LoRA finetuning on a relatively small (50K) dataset as an auxiliary shortcut, leaving it unclear how a pure Krause Attention model performs when pretrained from scratch for large-scale language modeling.

Hardware-level execution efficiency of the custom top-k and distance-based attention on GPUs is not discussed in depth. Standard GPUs are highly optimized for dot-product based matrix multiplication (e.g., FlashAttention), and computing Euclidean distances followed by a top-k step could introduce custom kernel overheads.

The qualitative text generation results in Table 21 (IFEval answers) show that the Krause-Llama3-8B response is highly repetitive, raising questions about the generation quality or degeneration under the proposed auxiliary path setting.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation connecting Transformer representation dynamics (e.g., representation collapse and attention sinks) to classical bounded-confidence opinion dynamics (the Krause consensus model).
Principled design that replaces global dot-product similarity with distance-based localized interactions, naturally achieving a linear time complexity of O(NWd).

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple modalities and architectures, including Vision Transformers (ViT, Swin) on ImageNet-1K, autoregressive image generation (MNIST, CIFAR-10), and Decoder-only LLMs (Llama3, Qwen1.5).
Clear presentation and high-quality visualizations (e.g., Figures 1, 3, 7, and 9) that effectively demonstrate the evolution of attention maps and the mitigation of attention sinks.
Thorough ablation studies (e.g., Table 13) that disentangle the individual contributions of the RBF kernel, local windowing, and top-k selection.
weaknesses: The practical implementation of top-k selection within a localized window can introduce sorting and selection overheads on modern GPU architectures. While the paper reports throughput improvements during inference, a detailed discussion or empirical validation of the actual training throughput and wall-clock times (e.g., training steps per second) compared to highly optimized implementations like FlashAttention is missing.

For large language models (LLMs), the proposed mechanism is only evaluated as an auxiliary shortcut trained via LoRA on top of pretrained models. It remains unclear whether Krause Attention can completely replace standard self-attention in a large-scale LLM pretrained from scratch, which is crucial for proving its viability as a fundamental alternative.

The computational complexity of the Euclidean distance in Eq. (5) requires calculating query and key norms or expanding the square, which can be computationally heavier than standard dot-product attention on modern hardware accelerators.

The comparison in language modeling (Table 6) involves a hybrid architecture where Krause Attention is added as an auxiliary path. The baseline LoRA setup has a 0.52% parameter overhead, while Krause-Llama has 0.59%. It is not fully clear if the gains are purely from Krause dynamics or the multi-pathway hybrid structure itself.

strengths: The paper introduces a mathematically elegant and principled attention mechanism, Krause Attention, grounded in the classical Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence consensus model, bridging the gap between dynamical systems and deep learning.

It addresses critical limitations of standard self-attention, such as representation collapse and the attention sink phenomenon, by replacing globally coupled dynamics with localized, distance-aware multi-cluster synchronization.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations are performed across diverse modalities—including vision (ViT on ImageNet-1K, CIFAR, Swin), autoregressive image generation (MNIST, CIFAR-10), and large language models (Llama3, Qwen) using LoRA—showing consistent performance gains alongside significant computation/FLOP reductions.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly intuitive visualizations and a solid theoretical analysis in the appendix linking the proposed attention to clustering emergence and mean-field dynamics.
weaknesses: For large language models, Krause Attention is only integrated as an auxiliary pathway via LoRA, rather than a full pre-trained replacement. This limits the demonstration of its capability to model long-range dependencies independently in the NLP domain.

The introduction of task-dependent hyperparameters (local window size $W$, top-$k$ sparsity, and the RBF kernel scale $\sigma$) adds tuning complexity, even though some empirical robustness is demonstrated.

The comparison to other modern sub-quadratic and sparse attention mechanisms (e.g., Neighborhood Attention or specialized sparse ViTs) is somewhat limited in the main experiments, which mostly compare against vanilla ViT/Swin baselines.
